## Verse-by-verse notes

**Title**
- "Chief Musician": some take this as God himself, others as a choir leader. VanGemeren (quoted by Guzik) says it probably marks the psalm for use in temple worship. EW
- Jeduthun was one of the musicians David appointed. Spurgeon (quoted by Guzik) notes that Jeduthun's sons were doorkeepers, and says good servants make the best singers. Guzik also says Scripture calls Asaph a prophet in his songs. EW
- Gill lists different views of "Jeduthun": the name of the chief musician, the first word of a tune (Aben Ezra), or the psalm's subject (the Midrash). He also lists different settings: the Babylonian exile (Theodoret), the time of Ahasuerus or Antiochus, or the church's last trouble under antichrist. His own view is that it describes the psalmist's personal case, which other believers share. GILL
- Ellicott thinks the trouble was national rather than personal, because all the comfort is drawn from the nation's history. He says the date can't be fixed, and he can't decide whether this psalm or Habakkuk 3:10–15 came first. GILL and ELL disagree here.
- Augustine reads the title symbolically: "Idithun" means "leaping over" and "Asaph" means "congregation." The speaker is the church, leaping over things in order to reach the end, which is Christ. AUG

**v. 1**
- Guzik: the psalmist cried out and knew God heard him. EW
- Gill: this is loud, urgent prayer spoken in distress. The repetition shows he prayed again and again, and God answers prayer as he promised (Ps 50:15). GILL
- Ellicott: the Hebrew is closer to "My voice to God — and let me cry." He says the KJV, following the ancient Greek and Latin versions, flattens the psalm's shifts of mood between outpouring and description. ELL
- Augustine: many people cry to God for wealth, safety or health, but hardly anyone cries for God himself. God truly hears you when you seek him, not when you use him to get something else. AUG

**v. 2**
- Guzik: the prayer was urgent, active and persistent. Hands stretched out was a Middle Eastern posture of prayer (VanGemeren). On "refused to be comforted," he says comfort is sometimes refused because it is shallow. He quotes Spurgeon: the psalmist turned comfort away like a sick man refusing food. He quotes Kidner, who hears an echo of Jacob refusing comfort over Joseph (Gen 37:35). He quotes Matthew Henry: trouble of mind must be prayed away, not drunk or laughed away. EW
- Gill: in trouble he sought the Lord, not other people or distractions. Trouble can come from our own sin, from persecution, from Satan, or from God withdrawing his presence. On the KJV's "my sore ran," he notes the Hebrew can mean "my hand" stretched out in prayer and not lowered, like Moses' hands (Ex 17:11). It is right to refuse false comfort built on our own merit, but wrong to refuse comfort from God's promises; doing so shows unbelief. GILL
- Ellicott: he thinks the Hebrew text here is damaged. "My hand was stretched out" is possible, and "eye" (tears) may be the original word. The KJV's "sore" comes from rabbis who pictured hands beating the breast. Whatever the wording, the anguish is clear. ELL

**v. 3**
- Guzik: he knew God heard him, yet he stayed troubled. When the trouble doesn't lift, feeling heard can bring more frustration, not less. He compares Paul's thorn in the flesh (2 Cor 12) and sees this as a struggle known to more mature believers. The "Selah" invites us to stop and reflect. EW
- Gill: remembering God troubled him. This could be because he remembered God's past kindness compared with now, or his own ungratefulness. Gill thinks it is most likely God's majesty and justice, seen as an angry Judge rather than a Father. GILL
- Ellicott translates "If I remember God I must sigh… my spirit faints," and says "overwhelmed" literally means "covers itself up." ELL

**v. 4**
- Guzik quotes Maclaren: it felt as if God's finger was holding his eyelids open. Clarke says being unable to speak shows the grief growing past words. EW
- Gill: the Hebrew is "the guards (eyelids) of my eyes." Losing sleep, which normally breaks up sorrow, is very distressing. He was speechless from weariness or from grief too big to say, or he didn't dare voice his thoughts. GILL
- Ellicott: better "Thou hast closed the guards of my eyes," and he says the KJV misreads the grammar. The word "troubled" is used elsewhere for being stunned by a mysterious dream (Gen 41:8; Dan 2:1), so the poet is too overawed to speak. ELL

**v. 5**
- Guzik: he wondered why God seemed to answer people in the past more fully than in the present. EW
- Gill: this could mean his own earlier life, or Israel's history going back to Adam, especially the Exodus. Reading Bible and church history can strengthen faith, but the good old days can also just make today feel worse (Eccl 7:10). GILL

**v. 6**
- Guzik: he remembered better times, and his searching was deep and careful. EW
- Gill: he tried to recall earlier songs of praise to lift his gloom, "but all to no purpose." He questioned his own heart to find the reason for God's dealings with him. GILL
- Ellicott: "Let me recall my harpings in the night… my spirit questions and questions." ELL

**vv. 7–9**
- Guzik: Asaph feared the dry season would last forever. He quotes Spurgeon, who says Asaph treated his unbelief "homeopathically," fighting questions with questions. Boice notes Spurgeon's own illness and depression, and Spurgeon said he knew Asaph's grief from experience. Clarke (on v. 9) says the picture is a spring whose mouth has been shut. The "Selah" again marks a hard honesty worth thinking about. EW
- Gill: the ancient versions differ. The Syriac states these lines as facts (the voice of unbelief), while the Targum reads "is it possible that…?" (the voice of faith). Through each verse Gill sets "Unbelief says…" against "Faith says…." God will not cast off those he foreknew. His mercy endures forever, and his promises never fail but are "yea and amen" in Christ. God cannot forget to be gracious. GILL
- Ellicott: God's silences frighten people more than his most terrible acts. To an Israelite used to God stepping in at the critical moment, a long delay felt like his protection had been withdrawn. ELL

**v. 10** (translations differ a lot here, so readers will notice)
- Guzik (NKJV "This is my anguish; but I will remember the years of the right hand"): this is the gap between belief and feeling, and he resolves to remember. Horne says faith begins to answer distrust. Spurgeon says memory is faith's helper, like Joseph opening the storehouses in famine. EW
- Gill gives three readings:
  1. Self-correction: "this is my infirmity," meaning his sin of doubting God.
  2. Comfort: this is a passing affliction allotted to him.
  3. "The changes of the right hand of the Most High" (Musculus, Ainsworth): God's hand is withdrawn for now, but it will change back.
  
  This third reading is closest to the BSB's "the right hand… has changed." GILL
- Ellicott says the word could mean "my wound or sickness." In that case, to keep despairing would be madness. But he prefers "profanation": despairing of a God who was gracious in the past is "a kind of blasphemy." ELL

**v. 11**
- Guzik: he remembers God's works, then meditates on them (v. 12), then talks about them. Kidner says "remember" here strictly means "make mention of," so it is a public telling. EW
- Gill: the written Hebrew means "I will cause to remember," that is, declare to others. Remembering what God has done, whether the Exodus or redemption in Christ, drives away doubt. GILL
- Ellicott: the written text means "I will celebrate." "Works" and "wonders" should be singular, meaning the one great rescue from Egypt. ELL

**v. 12**
- Gill: he meditates to imprint God's works on his own mind, and talks about them for the good of others and the glory of God (Ps 145:4). GILL

**v. 13** (NKJV/KJV "in the sanctuary"; BSB "is holy")
- Guzik: God's way "in the sanctuary" is the way to God through the blood of an innocent sacrifice, which ultimately points to Christ. EW
- Gill: it could be "in holiness" (the Syriac and Targum, "how holy are thy ways") or "in the sanctuary," where God explains his dealings to his people. GILL
- Ellicott: "with the holy," that is, with Israel, God's "saint." ELL

**v. 14**
- Guzik: God showed his strength again and again in Israel's history. EW
- Gill: he works wonders in nature, providence and grace, chiefly in Egypt and the wilderness. The nations heard about them. GILL

**v. 15**
- Kidner (quoted by Guzik): Jacob and Joseph are named together because both insisted that the Promised Land, not Egypt, must be their final rest. EW
- Gill: the rescue from Egypt is a type (a picture in advance) of redemption by Christ, "the arm… of God." Joseph is named for honour, as the one who kept the family alive and believed in their deliverance. GILL
- Ellicott: giving Joseph prominence is typical of the Asaph psalms. ELL

**v. 16**
- Guzik: the Red Sea is pictured as afraid of God. Horne says the waters are poetically given senses. EW
- Gill: this is the Red Sea, not the Jordan. He notes the old Syriac church read it as the Jordan at Christ's baptism, while Jerome read the "waters" as the nations (Rev 17:15). "Afraid" can mean "in pain," like a woman in labour. GILL
- Ellicott: there may be an allusion to the Lord "looking" on the Egyptians (Ex 14:24). "Afraid" is better translated "writhed, as in travail." ELL

**v. 17**
- Exodus doesn't mention a storm. Guzik leans toward taking it literally, quoting Josephus's account of rain, thunder and lightning. Boice says these are either details kept in Israel's memory or poetic additions, and either is plausible. Poole says the "arrows" are lightning or hail. EW
- Gill: the details are true because an inspired writer records them, and Josephus agrees (his page cuts off here). GILL
- Ellicott: Josephus and Philo both preserve the storm tradition. The "arrows" are lightnings darting back and forth. ELL

**v. 18**
- Guzik: the earth shaking is either extra information or poetic description. EW
- Ellicott: the Hebrew *galgal* is best rendered "in the vault [of heaven]," not "whirlwind" as modern scholars prefer. The ancient Greek and Latin versions have "wheel." ELL

**v. 19**
- Kidner (quoted by Guzik): this is a true picture of God's rule over nature, and as a man Jesus too had a path on the sea. Meyer says God wades through oceans as a man fords a stream. EW
- Ellicott quotes Stanley: we don't know the exact means or route of the rescue, and "we need not know." The mystery itself was part of the lesson. ELL

**v. 20**
- Guzik: God works both through great wonders and through ordinary human leaders, and one never excludes the other. Spurgeon: Egypt's attacker was Israel's shepherd. Meyer: the mighty God has a shepherd's tender heart. EW
- Ellicott: some think the abrupt ending means the psalm is unfinished, but he thinks it is the right ending. The answer to doubt is the faith and worship handed down through Moses and Aaron. If the psalm speaks for the community, the point is to stay loyal to those ancient institutions. ELL

## 2. Where the traditions differ
I couldn't reach any denominational site, so I can't tell you what Baptist, Methodist, Pentecostal, Reformed, Lutheran or Anglican teachers say from their own sources. What I can show is where the commentators I read disagree:
- **The setting:** personal (Gill) or national (Ellicott).
- **v. 10:** sin, affliction or "change" (Gill); "profanation" (Ellicott); "anguish" (Guzik).
- **v. 13:** sanctuary or holiness.
- **vv. 17–18:** whether the storm is literal.

## 3. Other views
- **Catholic/patristic:** only Augustine's reading of the title and verse 1 (AUG, above).
- **Ancient versions:** Gill and Ellicott report how the Septuagint (ancient Greek), Vulgate (Latin), Syriac and Targum (Aramaic) read several verses (above).
- **Not found:** the NET Bible notes, Bible Odyssey, Orthodox sources, and anything on prosperity, word-of-faith or hyper-grace teaching on this psalm.
